{{short description|Graph-based mathematical model}}
'''Phase-field models on graphs''' are a discrete analogue to [[phase-field models]], defined on a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]. They are used in [[image analysis]] (for feature identification) and for the segmentation of [[social network]]s.

== Graph Ginzburg–Landau functional ==
For a graph with vertices ''V'' and edge weights <math>\omega_{i,j}</math>, the graph Ginzburg–Landau functional of a map <math>u:V\to \mathbb{R}</math> is given by
:<math>F_\varepsilon(u) = \frac\varepsilon2 \sum_{i,j\in V} \omega_{ij} (u_i-u_j)^2 + \frac1\varepsilon \sum_{i \in V} W(u_i), 
</math>
where ''W'' is a double well potential, for example the quartic potential ''W''(''x'') = ''x''<sup>2</sup>(1 − ''x''<sup>2</sup>). The graph Ginzburg–Landau functional was introduced by Bertozzi and Flenner.<ref name="BF12">{{Cite journal |last1=Bertozzi |first1=A. |author-link=Andrea Bertozzi |last2=Flenner |first2=A. |date=2012-01-01 |title=Diffuse Interface Models on Graphs for Classification of High Dimensional Data |journal=Multiscale Modeling & Simulation |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=1090–1118 |doi=10.1137/11083109X |issn=1540-3459|citeseerx=10.1.1.299.4261 }}</ref> In analogy to continuum phase-field models, where regions with ''u'' close to 0 or 1 are models for two phases of the material, vertices can be classified into those with ''u''<sub>''j''</sub> close to 0 or close to 1, and for small <math>\varepsilon</math>, minimisers of <math>F_\varepsilon</math> will satisfy that ''u''<sub>''j''</sub> is close to 0 or 1 for most nodes, splitting the nodes into two classes.

== Graph Allen–Cahn equation ==
To effectively minimise <math>F_\varepsilon</math>, a natural approach is by [[gradient flow]] ([[steepest descent]]). This means to introduce an artificial time parameter and to solve the graph version of the [[Allen–Cahn equation]],
:<math>\frac{d}{dt} u_j = -\varepsilon (\Delta u)_j-\frac1\varepsilon W'(u_j),</math>
where <math>\Delta</math> is the [[Laplacian matrix|graph Laplacian]]. The ordinary continuum Allen–Cahn equation and the graph Allen–Cahn equation are natural counterparts, just replacing ordinary calculus by [[Calculus on finite weighted graphs|calculus on graphs]]. 
A convergence result for a numerical graph Allen–Cahn scheme has been established by Luo and Bertozzi.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luo |first1=Xiyang |last2=Bertozzi |first2=Andrea L. |date=2017-05-01 |title=Convergence of the Graph Allen–Cahn Scheme |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |language=en |volume=167 |issue=3 |pages=934–958 |doi=10.1007/s10955-017-1772-4 |bibcode=2017JSP...167..934L |issn=1572-9613|doi-access=free }}</ref>

It is also possible to adapt other computational schemes for [[mean curvature flow]], for example schemes involving [[thresholding (image processing)|thresholding]] like the Merriman–Bence–Osher scheme, to a graph setting, with analogous results.<ref>van Gennip, Yves. Graph Ginzburg–Landau: discrete dynamics, continuum limits, and applications. An overview. In {{Cite journal |last1=Ei |first1=S.-I. |last2=Giga |first2=Y. |last3=Hamamuki |first3=N. |last4=Jimbo |first4=S. |last5=Kubo |first5=H. |last6=Kuroda |first6=H. |last7=Ozawa |first7=T. |last8=Sakajo |first8=T. |last9=Tsutaya |first9=K. |date=2019-07-30 |title=Proceedings of 44th Sapporo Symposium on Partial Differential Equations |journal=Hokkaido University Technical Report Series in Mathematics |volume=177 |pages=89–102 |doi=10.14943/89899}}</ref>
